newsitem.title: IRAQ: Turkish troops chase rebel Kurds in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Turkish troops chase rebel Kurds in Iraq.

text.p: Thousands of Turkish troops, backed by tanks, heavy artillery and air power, pushed across the border into northern Iraq early on Wednesday in a move against separatist Kurdish rebel bases.

Witnesses said the assault, which began at 3 a.m. (2300 GMT) followed a security sweep by local Iraqi Kurdish authorities, who ordered all journalists to leave the border region, confiscated mobile telephones and film.
"Around 10,000 troops have crossed over from around Habur," said a Turkish official near the Habur border crossing.

He said they were heading northeast away from Zakho, the main town in the area, and had advanced up to 20 km (12 miles) into northern Iraq. The troops, including tanks and artillery, began crossing at 2300 GMT, according to witnesses.
The pro-Kurdish DEM news agency, based in Germany, said in a statement Turkish troops were bombarding hilltop positions in northern Iraq.

Turkey's state-run Anatolian news agency reported clashes between troops and the Turkish separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), in a region it called Sarisarilar. It said troops backed by U.S.-made Cobra helicopters had inflicted heavy losses on the PKK.
Baghdad demanded a withdrawal, saying the incursion breached international law. It said there were many casualties.

"The government of the Republic of Iraq vehemently condemns this new Turkish military aggression on the sovereignty of Iraq and its territorial integrity," the Iraqi news agency INA said, quoting a Foreign Ministry spokesman.
Britain said it was worried by the reports of the incursion.

"We support Turkey's aim of maintaining her own territorial integrity and protecting her legitimate security interests. We are urging the Turks not to exceed measures necessary to protect these interests," junior Foreign Office minister Doug Henderson said in a statement.
A Turkish Foreign Ministry spokesman said the operation was a "limited" one, in coordination with local Iraqi Kurds, to oust PKK guerrillas from the border marshes.

However, a senior security source told Reuters: "This is a wide and comprehensive operation." The border areas of northern Iraq have in the past been the scene of firefights between Turkish security forces and PKK guerrillas.
Defence Minister Turhan Tayan said the operation was a "humanitarian mission" to protect Iraqi Kurds from the PKK.
"The troops will withdraw when the operation is over," he told reporters. Turkish army officers in Iraq were tight-lipped.

A seven-km (four-mile) line of oil trucks, which regularly cross the border to buy cheap oil, extended back from the town of Cizre, some 45 km (30 miles) from the Iraqi border. Security forces were allowing no civilians the town, Reuters correspondent Daren Butler reported from Cizre.
Some military ambulances crossed the town on their way to Iraq. Security, always heavy in Cizre, was stepped up further.
"There is a news blackout. No member of the press is permitted access to Zakho," a local Iraqi Kurdish official said.
Turkish soldiers later enforced the news blackout, barring reporters from returning to the area.
The Iraqi side of the border is under the general control of Massoud Barzani's KDP, a rival of the separatist PKK.
An Iraqi opposition source told Reuters that the KDP had been fighting the PKK since Monday.
Northern Iraq was set up as a Western-backed autonomous Kurdish area following the 1991 Gulf War. The KDP and another Kurdish group have shared power, if acrimoniously, since then.
Barzani teamed up last year with forces of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein against rival Iraqi Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani, prompting U.S. missile strikes against Iraqi targets.

Turkish troops regularly cross back and forth in "hot pursuit" of the PKK. In March 1995, tens of thousands of troops pushed deep into Iraq for a prolonged campaign that drove the PKK back but failed to crush them.
Troops were also fighting the PKK within Turkey's borders. Security officials said troops had killed 30 Kurdish rebels in clashes in the southeast in the last two days.
More than 22,000 people have been killed in more than 12 years of fighting between the army and the PKK, which is seeking autonomy or independence in mainly Kurdish southeastern Turkey.
